title: Visual accessibility audit

sources.locator: Web Content Accessibility Guidelines 2.2; W3C Recommendation 2023; provisions applicable to Visual accessibility audit
sources.claim: Accessible CSS preserves visible focus, zoom and reflow, contrast, target size, reading order, user preferences, and content visibility.

canonicalExplanation.summary: Semantic HTML gives a good start, but **CSS can still create barriers**: hidden focus, low contrast, content clipped at zoom, text that doesn't reflow, information shown by colour alone, motion that ignores preferences, tiny touch targets. A visual accessibility audit checks these WCAG-informed points at **200% and 400% zoom**, in **forced colours**, with **reduced motion** and **keyboard only**, and records each finding with its fix.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
The sign-up form's HTML is perfect: labels, fieldsets, error messages. But at 200% zoom the two-column layout forces sideways scrolling, the focus ring is removed by a reset, and the error border is the only error signal. The CSS undid the HTML's good work. At 200 percent zoom a form reflows without two-dimensional scrolling and focus remains visible. In this lesson you'll record and repair findings from a WCAG-informed visual and interaction audit.

Can CSS still make the page inaccessible?", "options": ["No — accessibility lives in HTML", "Yes — CSS can hide focus, lower contrast, clip content and block reflow"], "answer": 1, "why": "Presentation matters: many WCAG criteria (contrast, reflow, focus visible, text spacing) are about how things look and move."}

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know the **Responsive design and motion** module, **Stylesheet organization**, **Color and contrast**, **Reduced motion and input preferences**, and **Overflow and containment**.

sections.heading: The model: a visual audit checklist
sections.body:
| Check | Pass when |
|---|---|
| focus visible. | every focusable element shows a clear :focus-visible style (≥ 3:1). |
| contrast. | text ≥ 4.5:1 (large 3:1); UI parts and focus ≥ 3:1. |
| reflow at 400% (320 CSS px). | no two-dimensional scrolling except tables/code. |
| zoom to 200%. | nothing clipped or overlapping. |
| text spacing. | extra line/letter/word spacing doesn't break layout. |
| not colour alone. | errors, links, states also use text/icons/underline. |
| motion. | reduced-motion preference honoured. |
| target size. | pointer targets at least 24×24 CSS px. |
| forced colours. | borders/focus still visible. |

**Finding format:** criterion · where · what fails · who's affected · fix · retest.

```reveal
{"prompt": "What does \"reflow\" mean in practice?", "answer": "At 320 CSS pixels wide (roughly 400% zoom on a laptop), content should fit in one column and scroll only vertically — no hunting sideways for the end of each line."}
```

sections.heading: Repair in CSS

includes: Audit CSS against focus, contrast, reflow, zoom, spacing, colour-only, motion and target-size checks.
Record findings and repair them in the stylesheet.

outcomes: Record and repair findings from a WCAG-informed visual and interaction audit.

examples.title: A form at 200% zoom
examples.situation: At 200 percent zoom a form reflows without two-dimensional scrolling and focus remains visible.
walkthrough: **Audit at 200% zoom:** the two-column grid forces sideways scrolling; the reset hides focus; errors use only a red border. Three findings recorded.
**Repair:** the grid becomes `repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(100%, 16rem), 1fr))`, `:focus-visible` gets a 3px outline with 3:1 contrast, and errors gain text plus an icon.
**Retest:** at 200% and 400% zoom the browser will render one reflowing column with no two-dimensional scrolling, and focus remains visible on every field.
examples.result: The form reflows at high zoom, shows focus everywhere, and signals errors beyond colour.

examples.title: The tiny icon buttons
examples.situation: A toolbar has 16×16px icon buttons packed tightly together. Users with tremors tap the wrong one.
walkthrough: The targets are below the 24×24 CSS px minimum with no spacing.
Fix: `min-width: 2.75rem; min-height: 2.75rem` (44px) or padding around the icons, plus a gap.
examples.result: Targets are large enough to hit reliably with a finger or a shaky pointer.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Accessibility is handled entirely by semantic HTML, so CSS cannot create barriers.
misconceptions.correction: CSS controls focus visibility, contrast, reflow, spacing, motion and target size. A page with perfect HTML can still fail users if its styles hide focus, clip content or rely on colour alone.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In "A form at 200% zoom", which three barriers did the CSS create?

analogy.example: HTML is the **building's structure** (ramps, lifts); CSS is the **lighting, signage and furniture**. A building with ramps can still be unusable if the lights are off and furniture blocks the doors.
limitations: Buildings don't zoom; pages must reflow.
Signage colour alone isn't enough — like colour-only errors.

artifact: apply fixes: auto-fit grid, :focus-visible, error text + icon

remediation.explanation: Run the checklist in this order: **keyboard focus → contrast → 200%/400% zoom → text spacing → colour-only → motion → target size → forced colours**. Write each failure down before fixing.

recap.summary: To record and repair findings from a WCAG-informed visual and interaction audit, check focus visibility, contrast, reflow at 200% and 400% zoom, text spacing, colour-only signals, motion preferences, target size and forced colours — then fix each in CSS and retest.
